summary.text: For \(n=2,3,4\), the congruence \(10^i\equiv1+9i\pmod{81}\) shows that any admissible smaller multiple has digit sum divisible by \(3^n\); the digit-sum bound then forces its digits all to be 9, while direct arithmetic checks establish divisibility of the corresponding all-nines candidates. For \(n=5+j\), start with the palindromic multiple \(29799999792\) of \(3^5\) and repeatedly concatenate three copies: each step preserves palindromicity and supplies another factor of 3, while its \(11\cdot3^j\) digits are fewer than the \(27\cdot3^j\) digits of the all-nines number, giving a strictly smaller admissible value.

full_proof.text:
Let \(R(m)\) denote the integer obtained by reversing the decimal digits of \(m\). Leading zeroes produced by the reversal are, as usual, discarded. For a positive integer \(N\), the sequence value \(a(N)\) is the least positive multiple \(kN\), with \(k\ge 1\), such that \(N\mid R(kN)\), if such a multiple exists; otherwise it is \(0\).

We prove that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\),
\[
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\in\{2,3,4\}.
\]

The proof has two parts. First we prove the equality for \(n=2,3,4\), including the required minimality. Then, for every \(n\ge 5\), we construct a much smaller positive multiple of \(3^n\) which is a palindrome and hence whose reversal is also divisible by \(3^n\).

## 1. A digit-sum lemma modulo powers of 3

We first establish the key fact used for the three exceptional exponents.

**Digit-sum lemma.** Let \(0\le t\le 4\), and suppose that both a positive integer \(m\) and its decimal reversal \(R(m)\) are divisible by \(3^t\). Then the sum of the decimal digits of \(m\) is divisible by \(3^t\).

To prove this, write the decimal digits of \(m\), starting with the least significant digit, as
\[
d_0,d_1,\ldots,d_{r-1},
\]
where \(0\le d_i\le 9\) and \(d_{r-1}\ne0\). Thus
\[
m=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}d_i10^i,
\qquad
R(m)=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}d_i10^{r-1-i}.
\]
This second formula remains correct even when \(d_0=0\), because an initial zero in the reversed digit string contributes nothing.

Since
\[
10=1+9,
\]
we have, for every \(i\ge0\),
\[
10^i\equiv 1+9i\pmod {81}.
\]
For example, this follows immediately by induction: if \(10^i\equiv1+9i\pmod{81}\), then
\[
10^{i+1}\equiv(1+9i)(1+9)
=1+9(i+1)+81i
\equiv1+9(i+1)\pmod{81}.
\]
Because \(3^t\mid81\) for \(t\le4\), the same congruence holds modulo \(3^t\).

Let
\[
S=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}d_i
\]
be the digit sum. Applying the congruence to \(m\) and its reversal gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
m+R(m)
&\equiv \sum_{i=0}^{r-1}d_i\bigl((1+9i)+(1+9(r-1-i))\bigr)\\
&=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}d_i\bigl(2+9(r-1)\bigr)\\
&=\bigl(2+9(r-1)\bigr)S
\pmod{3^t}.
\end{aligned}
\]
By hypothesis, the left side is \(0\) modulo \(3^t\). The coefficient \(2+9(r-1)\) is congruent to \(2\) modulo \(3\), so it is relatively prime to \(3^t\). It is therefore invertible modulo \(3^t\). Consequently
\[
S\equiv0\pmod{3^t},
\]
which proves the lemma.

We will also use the following elementary extremal fact about digit sums.

**Maximum digit-sum fact.** If \(0<m<10^L\), then the digit sum \(S(m)\) satisfies
\[
S(m)\le 9L.
\]
Moreover, equality can occur only for
\[
m=10^L-1,
\]
the number consisting of exactly \(L\) nines.

Indeed, \(m<10^L\) means that \(m\) has at most \(L\) decimal digits, and every digit is at most \(9\), proving the bound. If the sum is \(9L\), there must be exactly \(L\) digits and every one of them must equal \(9\). Thus the number is \(99\ldots 9=10^L-1\).

## 2. The equality for \(n=2,3,4\)

Fix \(n\in\{2,3,4\}\), and put
\[
N=3^n,
\qquad
L=3^{n-2},
\qquad
A=10^L-1.
\]
The number \(A\) consists of \(L\) nines, so it is a palindrome and hence
\[
R(A)=A.
\]
Also,
\[
9L=9\cdot3^{n-2}=3^2\cdot3^{n-2}=3^n=N.
\]

For the three possible values of \(n\), direct arithmetic gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
n&N&L&A\\ \hline
2&9&1&9=9\cdot1,\\
3&27&3&999=27\cdot37,\\
4&81&9&999{,}999{,}999=81\cdot12{,}345{,}679.
\end{array}
\]
Thus in every case \(N\mid A\). Since \(R(A)=A\), the number \(A\) is an admissible multiple in the definition of \(a(N)\). It remains to prove that no smaller positive multiple is admissible.

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that there is a positive integer \(m<A\) such that
\[
N\mid m
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
N\mid R(m).
\]
Because \(n\le4\), the digit-sum lemma shows that
\[
N\mid S(m),
\]
where \(S(m)\) is the sum of the decimal digits of \(m\).

Since
\[
m<A=10^L-1<10^L,
\]
the maximum digit-sum fact gives
\[
S(m)\le9L=N.
\]
Also \(m>0\), so its digit sum is positive. Therefore \(S(m)\) is a positive multiple of \(N\) not exceeding \(N\), and hence
\[
S(m)=N=9L.
\]
Equality in the digit-sum bound forces
\[
m=10^L-1=A,
\]
contradicting \(m<A\).

Therefore \(A\) is the least positive multiple of \(N\) whose reversal is also divisible by \(N\). We have proved
\[
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\]
for \(n=2,3,4\).

## 3. A family of smaller palindromic multiples for every \(n\ge5\)

We now construct positive palindromes \(P_j\), for \(j\ge0\), with the following properties:
\[
3^{5+j}\mid P_j,
\qquad
R(P_j)=P_j,
\qquad
P_j<10^{11\cdot3^j}.
\]

Begin with the eleven-digit palindrome
\[
P_0=29{,}799{,}999{,}792.
\]
Its digit string is
\[
29799999792,
\]
which reads the same in either direction. A direct division gives
\[
P_0=243\cdot122{,}633{,}744=3^5\cdot122{,}633{,}744.
\]
Thus \(P_0\) is a positive palindrome divisible by \(3^5\).

Inductively, obtain \(P_{j+1}\) by concatenating three copies of the complete decimal digit string of \(P_j\). If that string has length \(\ell_j\), then
\[
P_{j+1}
=P_j\bigl(1+10^{\ell_j}+10^{2\ell_j}\bigr).
\]
At the initial stage \(\ell_0=11\), and tripling the block triples its length, so
\[
\ell_j=11\cdot3^j.
\]
No leading-zero issue arises, since the leading digit of the original block is \(2\), and every subsequent block begins with the same digit.

The concatenation of three identical palindromic blocks is again a palindrome: reversing it reverses both the order of the three blocks and each individual block, but all three blocks are equal and each is fixed by reversal. Hence, inductively,
\[
R(P_j)=P_j
\]
for every \(j\ge0\).

We next prove the asserted divisibility. The base case \(3^5\mid P_0\) was calculated above. Suppose that
\[
3^{5+j}\mid P_j.
\]
Since \(10\equiv1\pmod3\), we have
\[
1+10^{\ell_j}+10^{2\ell_j}
\equiv1+1+1
\equiv0\pmod3.
\]
Therefore the extra factor in the formula for \(P_{j+1}\) is divisible by \(3\), and so
\[
3^{5+j+1}\mid P_{j+1}.
\]
By induction,
\[
3^{5+j}\mid P_j
\]
for all \(j\ge0\).

Finally, because \(P_j\) has exactly \(11\cdot3^j\) decimal digits,
\[
0<P_j<10^{11\cdot3^j}.
\]

Now let \(n\ge5\), and set
\[
j=n-5.
\]
Then \(n=5+j\), so the divisibility just proved says
\[
3^n=3^{5+j}\mid P_j.
\]
Since \(P_j\) is a palindrome,
\[
R(P_j)=P_j,
\]
and hence its reversal is also divisible by \(3^n\). Thus \(P_j\) is an admissible positive multiple in the definition of \(a(3^n)\), and consequently
\[
a(3^n)\le P_j.
\]

It remains to compare \(P_j\) with the proposed all-nines value. Since
\[
n-2=(5+j)-2=j+3,
\]
we have
\[
3^{n-2}=3^{j+3}=27\cdot3^j.
\]
On the other hand, \(P_j\) has \(11\cdot3^j\) digits. Because \(11<27\),
\[
11\cdot3^j<27\cdot3^j=3^{n-2}.
\]
It follows that
\[
P_j<10^{11\cdot3^j}<10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
\]
For the final strict inequality, note that the two exponents are integers with the second at least one larger than the first; hence \(10^{11\cdot3^j}\le10^{3^{n-2}-1}<10^{3^{n-2}}-1\).

Combining the last two estimates gives
\[
a(3^n)\le P_j<10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
\]
Therefore
\[
a(3^n)\ne10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\]
for every \(n\ge5\).

## 4. Conclusion

For \(n=2,3,4\), Section 2 proves
\[
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
\]
Conversely, if \(n\ge2\) but \(n\notin\{2,3,4\}\), then necessarily \(n\ge5\), and Section 3 proves that this equality is impossible. Hence, for every integer \(n\ge2\),
\[
\boxed{
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\in\{2,3,4\}.
}
\]
